INTRO: Let's zoom into one of our account shards.
PRIMARY_AND_REPLICA: It has a Primary and a replica.
PRIMARY_OWNS: The Primary owns changes to that shard's accounts.
PRIMARY_FAIL: Now imagine it suddenly becomes unavailable.
REQUEST_FAILURE: Requests for accounts on this shard begin to fail or wait.
OTHER_SHARD: Accounts belonging to another healthy shard may still be served.
RECOVERY_PATH: The replica gives us a possible recovery path.
PROMOTE: We can promote an eligible replica to become the new Primary.
LEGITIMATE_OWNER: But before the new Primary starts accepting writes, the system must establish that it is the legitimate owner.
OLD_RETURN: Because the old Primary might return.
TWO_WRITERS: Imagine the old Primary accepting one account change while the newly promoted Primary accepts another.
FENCING: A safe design needs coordination and fencing:
FENCE_MEANING: a way to prevent the former Primary from continuing to act as the writer after ownership has changed.
DATA_RISK: But there is one more risk.
LAG: The replica might not have received every recent committed change before the original Primary failed.
DATA_LOSS: So promoting it could mean losing some recent data.
GREEN_ARROW: This is why failover cannot be treated as simply changing a green arrow on a diagram.
CORRECTNESS: It is a decision about ownership, recovery and correctness.
INSTANCES: More database instances can help the system survive a failure.
WRONG_STATE: But availability is not enough if the system recovers into the wrong account state.
TEST_FAILURES: The only way to trust this architecture is to test those failures before users experience them.
